speaker: The Chairman
text: Head L, the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I do hope he does this more often and calls my name; my correct name more often as well.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But for that occasion, I really did not raise my hand and I replied to him that, for once, I have no questions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I had no questions as I sincerely believe that we are heading in the right direction in terms of our climate policies.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is no doubt there is still work to be done but we have done so much in the past few years to not just adapt to climate change but, most importantly, mitigate climate change.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are significantly cutting our emissions and getting everyone on board on this important journey to save our planet.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have also done a phenomenal job in our #SayYesToWasteLess campaign and for all of us to go zero waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are also taking active steps to solve problems we all face on the ground.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We will be more effective in tackling high rise litter with the recent amendments to the Environmental Public Health Act and Project Wolbachia is proving a vital tool in our efforts to combat dengue.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are also uplifting our lower income workers with the Progressive Wage Model (PWM) for workers in our cleaning and waste management sectors.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We are also doing well in advancing food resilience and security, ensuring water sustainability and transforming and uplifting the hawker industry.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Now that we done so much and done so well in all the above aspects, we now have some breathing space and some time to devote to tackling second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Our residents need their breathing space and need us to change our policies so they can protect themselves and their loved ones from the dangers of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like climate change, you cannot just adapt to secondhand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like complaints about high-rise littering, complaints about secondhand smoke is rising, it is doubled.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: And like high-rise littering, we need to amend our policies and even our laws to tackle secondhand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Like Project Wolbachia, we can be creative and come up with ways to detect, deter and wipe out secondhand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know Senior Minister of State Amy Khor is equally concerned about secondhand smoke and I know that we can move forward on this issue like so many other issues I have debated her in this House over the years.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I know my Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) colleagues, fellow Members of Parliament and I will be asking lots more questions and I look forward to a robust debate.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: It has been two years since the Singapore Green Plan 2030 was launched.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The plan touches every aspect of our lives and requires a whole-of-nation effort to attain its sustainable development goals.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: Although it was only launched two years ago, Singapore, our Clean and Green City, has been laying the foundation for this movement over the decades.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: What are the key challenges which lay ahead?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: The Green Plan requires many capabilities to be established in many public agencies.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San (Sembawang)
text: How is the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) organising its resources to balance the business-as-usual requirements versus the challenges faced in implementing the Green Plan?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Government provide an update on our progress of GreenGov.SG and what lies ahead?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Don Wee, you could take your two cuts together, please.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Under GreenGov.SG, the public sector aims to reach ambitious sustainability targets in carbon abatement and resource efficiency as well as influence support and enable green efforts nationwide, whether these are initiated by individuals, community groups or the private sector.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Specific targets are set for buildings, information technology (IT), transport and solar deployment.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Public sector infrastructure and operations, such as public transport, infrastructure and healthcare facilities, are included.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Will such efforts entail higher costs, leading to higher fees?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If so, what measures are there to mitigate these increases, particularly in view of the inflationary environment currently?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In addition, how will the Minister ensure that the public sector's organs, Ministries, and statutory boards meet the set targets?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would MSE share how GreenGov.SG will work with Singaporeans and residents and the private sector to reach its ambitious goals?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Can the Government provide an update on our progress so far and what lies ahead?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Ministry had shared that to enable a sustainable economy, it would require the public sector to engage in green procurement.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, products must meet high efficiency or sustainability standards.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This requirement will apply to a very wide range, from electrical appliances to building materials.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am curious how wide the scope would be and to what extent items will be evaluated.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For example, as meat accounts for nearly 60% of all greenhouse gases from food production, does it mean less meat at events organised by the public sector?

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I look forward to the public sector's green procurement becoming an exciting new opportunity for our home-grown companies.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is very important to support our SMEs as the public sector transits to green procurement.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: SMEs may face significant obstacles in their attempts to bid for and win public procurement contracts for many reasons, including their limited resources, lack of knowledge about the new green requirements, unfamiliarity with possibly lengthy and difficult bidding processes and so on.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I appeal to the Government to make an effort during this transition phase to provide support for our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Don Wee (Chua Chu Kang)
text: How is the Government driving green procurement, so as to help SMEs and to engender a green economy?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Public Service is one of the biggest users of services in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Its procurement contracts are very significant in value.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Public agencies abide by the procurement principles of transparency, open and fair competition and value for money.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: For many years, I have called for sustainability to be included as a principle of Government procurement.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have also called to expand life cycle costing to more categories of products, by measuring and setting standards for carbon footprint and publishing a yearly sustainability report.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Many of our Government contractors also service other clients.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: When we tighten our sustainability requirements, it can spark process improvements across the supply chain, creating a multiplier effect.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Government share how it is driving green procurement to create a green economy?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Will the Government introduce a green procurement roadmap similar to our carbon tax roadmap to help businesses prepare and change mindsets much earlier?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: This includes ensuring that sustainability principles are considered in our business practices and processes across all sectors.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: How is the Government encouraging the practice of green procurement, which is the purchase of goods and services that caused minimal adverse environmental impact as part of building and supporting a green economy for Singapore?

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: The objective of mandatory climate disclosures is to ensure that the impact of our actions on climate change are systematically and thoroughly recorded in our work, business and investment decisions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: Having actual data tracked routinely will help our organisations to get a better understanding of their choices in the course of their actions, enabling them to make better decisions in the future.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: This will lead to a more responsible and efficient allocation of resources and capital as well as to expedite Singapore's transition to become a more sustainable nation with low carbon emissions.

speaker: Mr Don Wee
text: This will also help us meet our international obligations and attain our net-zero carbon target in time.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: The investment market and customers have demanded a greater transparency for useful climate change risks and opportunities information related to businesses.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: In a way, this demand has become so strong that businesses that fail to disclose their climate change risks could jeopardise their reputations.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, reputational risk do not solely apply to businesses only, they have similar implications for any Government.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: First, the need for disclosure from businesses and Government.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, there has not been any requirement made on the Government and its agencies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While we have the intended strategies in place as a nation, we also need instruments to monitor and measure against the targets set on a continuous basis.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As the Government is the regulator and governing structure in Singapore, are there any plans for the Government to provide similar disclosures annually, in order to send strong signals about our commitment to combat climate change?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Second, the provisioning and allocation of allowances for carbon emissions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Given how heavily trade exposed our economy is, such a provision is vital to ensure our businesses remain competitive as they adjust towards a low-carbon economy.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: However, the Act does not define clear boundaries on how much allowances the Government will be allowed to issue and how these will be allocated from a sectorial perspective.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: This brings me to the point about volume of allowance, its fair allocation and integrity of businesses using the allowance.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How will the volume be calibrated over the years as Singapore progressively lowers our carbon intensity?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Will the Ministry consider introducing a cap on the number of allowances that can be issued annually to safeguard against any overprovision of allowances from a national perspective?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: On the allocation of allowances, could the Minister also clarify how the Government plans to allocate allowances across the different sectors?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: As the businesses liable for carbon tax can have differing strategic importance to Singapore, how will the Government benchmark a business which provides critical infrastructure, such as the power sector, versus another business which serves as a growth engine in new emerging economy?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: While the current provision allows internationally recognised benchmarks to be applied in the methodology of assessing the award of allowances, it does not obligate the use of benchmarking elements.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: Will there be regular benchmarking reviews on its carbon intensity performance against global peers?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling (East Coast)
text: How would feedback loops be put in place to adjust the allowances issued based on the benchmarking results?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: But as at July 2022, its take-up rate remains relatively low.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: What is the Government doing to improve the take-up rate of this programme?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Chairman, with the green transition, there will be a learning curve for companies and workers, and both must meet new conditions.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some businesses may be unable to keep up while others will find new opportunities.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Some workers will be made redundant, but others will find themselves in high demand for their new expertise.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Even households are not spared from needing to adapt to greening.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: They must learn new habits to save water and electricity, reduce and recycle waste, for example.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How will the Government support businesses, households and individuals with the green transition?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: With increasing inflationary pressures, households are looking for ways to cut down on expenditures, including on utility bills.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Switching to more energy-saving appliances would require investments in new ones.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Any effort to reach our net-zero greenhouse gas emission target must surely require their active involvement.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: What has the Ministry been and is doing to help SMEs become more energy-efficient?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The Government has been advocating the use of more energy-efficient air conditioners, lighting and household appliances with energy efficiency ratings so consumers can be better informed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What accounts for the 33% increase in electricity of Singapore households over the last 10 years?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What more can the Ministry do now to help Singapore households manage their electricity consumption?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the targeted electricity consumption by each Singapore household that the Ministry hopes to achieve and how is this target communicated to the public?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our Public Service and commercial industries are major consumers of the remaining 85%.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: What is the Ministry now doing to make them more energy-efficient and reduce electricity consumption?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Chairman, I am proud of Singapore's achievement in being amongst the very few countries in the world to have closed the water loop and reuse our water resources repeatedly.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Our water treatment infrastructure and technologies have enabled us to move towards long-term water sustainability.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With COVID-19, the timelines of various infrastructure projects were delayed due to manpower shortages and supply chain disruptions.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: When is PUB expecting to complete Phase 2 of the DTSS project?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: On a related note, would the Minister share an update on the progress of the Tuas Water Reclamation Plant as well as the Kranji Water Reclamation Plant?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Apart from the DTSS and Tuas and Kranji plants, are there new used water treatment plants in the plans?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How will such developments improve Singapore's water supply resilience?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Correspondingly, with the increase in electricity tariffs and the Public Sector's goal to achieve net zero earlier by 2045, how will these pressures affect the cost and quantity of NEWater production?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How does PUB intend to commercialise and scale up promising technologies in Singapore and overseas?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, the non-domestic sector uses about 55% of Singapore's water supply.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: This proportion is expected to increase to 70% by 2060.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: PUB introduced the Mandatory Water Efficiency Management Practices (MWEMP) for non-domestic users in 2015.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Has MWEMP been effective in improving their water efficiency and what measures does PUB have to motivate further improvements?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Prof Koh, kindly take your four cuts together.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Recently, Minister Grace Fu assured the House that the Government will take all scrutiny of carbon markets and projects seriously and is finalising a list of international carbon credits that companies in Singapore may use for offsetting their emissions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Will the Government share the quality considerations and criteria for identifying eligible carbon projects' host countries, carbon crediting programmes and carbon accounting methodologies for carbon tax offsets in Singapore?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Last year, the Government launched the Forward Singapore exercise to engage all segments of society to discuss the challenges, constraints and opportunities that Singapore faces as we move forward to realise our common vision for the future.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Can the Government provide an update on the Steward Pillar of Forward Singapore and how Singaporeans are wanting to contribute towards a green, liveable and climate-resilient Singapore?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Since 2019, the National Environment Agency's (NEA) "Say YES to Waste Less" campaign has introduced initiatives to reduce food wastage and discourage the use of disposables such as bags, cups and takeout containers.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Recently, NEA commissioned a campaign called The Waste Cafe, which generated some negative feedback from the public.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: How is the Government ensuring that future campaigns that seek to create public awareness, sometimes understandably through a shock factor, will not inadvertently lead to unnecessary waste?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Will the Government share the outcomes of this campaign?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Domestic recycling is an important part of Singapore's sustainability journey.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Can the Government share the outcomes of initiatives such as the pilot programme involving transparent recycling bins and dedicated recycling chutes in HDB blocks?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Ensuring greater buy-in and success of our domestic recycling efforts is key to achieving Singapore's zero-waste ambitions and plans to turn trash to treasure.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Will the Government consider other recycling initiatives, such as getting households to sort their waste at home?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Items containing food and liquid waste are frequently sighted being disposed of in recycling bins.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Despite NEA's Recycle Right campaign, we still continue to see non-recyclable items such as used shoes and textiles found in these recycling bins.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: During the GAC's deep dive, green task force members from my Woodgrove division also shared with me that the issue of reducing household waste and successful recyclables are intertwined.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The reduction of waste and contamination rates begin at home.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Residents need to be equipped with the knowledge on what kinds of waste can be reduced, reused and recycled.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: While sorting is not required in Singapore as separation of materials is done at the materials recovery facilities, not doing so increases the likelihood of recyclables being contaminated.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Voluntary Welfare Organisations (VWOs) like Tzu Chi Foundation has set a good standard for us to follow.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: By setting up active recycling points, residents will be more empowered to take matters into their own hands, putting in the effort to segregate all waste materials.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Can the Ministry explore how we can eventually do away with one physical recycle bin but adopt methods practised in countries such as Japan by setting up more active recycling points and allowing a certain day of the week to be set aside as the recycling collection day when residents can place their segregated items for recycling?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, more Singaporeans are now conscious of climate change and the need for sustainability.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We see more people bringing their own shopping bags and recycling.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Singaporeans are used to collecting and using such plastic bags for the disposal of trash and waste.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How do we balance the need to cut down on plastic bags and the need to contain trash?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How is the response so far for the collection of e-waste and recyclables via the big blue bins in our housing estates?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Has the problem of contamination of the bins been reduced?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How can the Ministry encourage more responsible usage of these bins?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Louis Ng, please take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It is an issue close to my heart as I see so much wastage of precious resources.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: E-waste that is improperly handled can also be toxic and damage the environment.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am glad we are finally seeing progress in terms of tackling e-waste.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: E-waste bins are now a common sight in our neighbourhoods and malls.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) System for e-waste ensures the proper handling of e-waste and that valuable resources can be extracted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Ministry share what other measures it is studying to further increase e-waste recycling rates?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It has been almost five years since I delivered an Adjournment Motion to call for a charge on single-use carrier bags.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Five years later, this has become a reality and we will soon be debating a Bill to make a disposable carrier bag charge at supermarkets compulsory.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Many supermarkets and shops have already started to charge for disposable bags.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am glad that many Singaporeans have adapted to this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I often see shoppers bring their own reusable bags or decline to take disposable bags for small items.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I believe we are starting to see a mindset shift.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Ministry share whether we will look into extending the requirements to convenience stores?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: In particular, the small disposable carrier bags for small convenience stores purchases are often unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am sure Senior Minister of State Amy Khor is tired of hearing me repeat myself and of repeating her replies even though she just told me that she is immune to it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I continue to raise the issue of second-hand smoke because it continues to be a problem many people face and people continue to have no solutions that will protect them from the dangers of second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Second-hand smoke kills and is a public health issue rather than a neighbourly dispute.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Many times, we tell our residents that the Community Disputes Resolution Tribunals (CDRT) may be a solution.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: She shared how even a CDRT court order was powerless to help protect her family from second-hand smoke.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: She shared the following in a forum letter, “A chain-smoking neighbour exposes my family to smoke every single day.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: The exposure to toxic second-hand smoke has greatly affected our health, living and lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: My mother often suffers from coughing and throat irritation, which make it difficult for her to eat as she chokes easily.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: We obtained a court order from the CDRT in June 2022, but this was not enough to stop the smoking.” To help Ms Chong and so many other residents, can the Ministry conduct a public consultation and set up a citizens’ workgroup to study the issue of second-hand smoke in homes?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Indeed, even before the current escalating food prices, it is rare to find many countries having such dining options with a smorgasbord of cuisines to choose from at comparable price points.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: It is no wonder that many overseas visitors rave about Singapore’s hawker centre – not just about its tasty food and variety, but also commenting that the prices are reasonable.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: However, for many Singaporeans and families who have their daily meals in our hawker centres and coffee shops, they found the price increases since the pandemic, and now with inflation, something hard to accept as they felt the prices will only trend upwards in future.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: The question is with several measures already in place on the national level to mitigate the effects of rising food prices, are these sufficient or are there other factors which impact food affordability that still needs to be addressed?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: With the increased number of hawker centres, how do we ensure there are sufficient hawkers joining this trade in order to sustain it?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Further, is the issue today one that we can rebalance by having more supply or options for consumers in each geographical area or is it one that needs relooking at where hawkers continue to have reasonable profit margins so that they can earn their living wage while serving the masses?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I seek more clarity from the Minister in these areas.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Chairman, the COVID-19 pandemic, disruptions to the global supply chain, the Russian-Ukraine war, extreme weather conditions, amongst others, all contribute to the sustained inflation which our world is facing today.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many food and beverage (F&B) establishments, including our hawker stalls, have had to increase prices due to the rising costs of ingredients, as well as higher utility bills.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: When I do my walkabouts in the hawker centres in my constituency, residents highlight to me that food is now very expensive.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Many suggest that the Government reduce the rentals so that hawkers can maintain or lower their prices.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a nation which needs to import most of our food ingredients, energy and even water, there is little we can do for these components.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the rentals, at least at hawker centres, is something which the Ministry has control over.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How is the Government supporting hawkers during this challenging period to ensure that our hawker food remains affordable?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One suggestion I have is the building of more hawker centres in the areas where a large number of Singaporeans work at.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, people who work in the Marina Bay Area have few choices for cheaply priced lunches.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Not everyone who works in the Marina Bay Area is a wealthy banker.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Assistant deliverymen, cleaners, coffee ladies, new entrants into the workforce and many others in junior positions have to work and eat lunch there and those in junior positions usually have very restricted lunch times and cannot travel far for lunch before having to get back to the office.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: One person told me that his daughter is happy that she recently moved from working at Marina Boulevard to working at Havelock Road where she has many more reasonable options for lunch that are easy to get to.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is one area where the Government can directly intervene – build hawker centres in areas where people work and keep rentals down, so that we can help hawkers in turn keep prices down.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is a way to keep everyday costs low for Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Chairman, in Singapore, hawker centres have been and will continue to serve the diverse needs of communities in residential, recreational, and work districts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Being a social space that embraces people from diverse socio-economic backgrounds, hawker centres play a crucial role in enhancing community interactions and strengthening the social fabric.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am encouraged to hear that the Ministry has been doing much over the years to not only keep the barriers to entry low, through keeping rents reasonable and by not requiring minimum bids during monthly stall tender exercises, but also to attract new talent and nurture the next generations of hawkers.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Beyond providing affordable food options and telling stories of our heritage, they also form communal spaces.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Has the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) assessed the demand for hawker centres and wet markets in the near future in different areas and will the newly open hawker centres in the next few years be able to meet this demand?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is also important to help existing hawker centres keep up with the times.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How are we ensuring that both new and older hawker centres are sustainable and does MSE have plans to enhance hawker centres with older structures and consider using new innovations to tackle other issues such as urban bird challenges?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Chairman, the Hawkers Go Digital Programme has seen an increase in SGQR transactions at participating stalls.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Would the Ministry share an update on the growth of SGQR transactions, and the Singapore Together Alliance for Action – Online Ordering for Hawkers scheme?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What more could be done to support our hawkers with the use of digitalisation to improve business and productivity?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: The COVID-19 pandemic has taught us many lessons, including a few on the resilience of our food supply framework.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: We learnt the importance of having homegrown sources and diverse suppliers from all over the world.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: What plans does the Ministry have to ensure the resilience, affordability and accessibility of our food supply?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Chairman, we are a small nation state and reliant on many imports for our survival.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The pandemic showed us how food insecurity could pose a real concern.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We worried for our food supply and other essentials when countries suddenly imposed lockdowns to the movement of people and goods.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: The disruptions have seen how essential goods were stuck at logistic centres, warehouses or ports because the workforce was unable to man the operations, for one reason or another, or the shipping and air routes were closed.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Fortunately, we were not caught off guard suddenly as we had in the past years worked hard to expand our sources of food supply, reaching out to countries from Brazil to Poland and South Africa, and from China to Australia besides our neighbouring countries.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Minister update the House on how the "30 by 30" strategy has been progressing?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What is the Government doing now to help our local importers become more robust and resilient against any food supply shocks?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: How is the response to the grants and land tenders for other food items apart from hen shell eggs, food, fish and leafy vegetables?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Are we making good progress in novel future food such as cultured meats?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What can be done to get our consumers to be more resilient towards food supply disruptions?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Chairman, with an increasingly volatile climate pattern and supply disruptions, COVID-19 has only reiterated the importance for Singapore to enhance our self-reliance in basic supplies.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Yet, that is only the starting point to convert existing farms and solutions.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: This includes impact on land and water resources, studies on the life cycle of different breeds of fish and crustaceans, health of each breed under varying environmental conditions, how to manage controlled parameters for healthy breed of produce, availability of efficacious vaccines for intervention and to promote growth of fry and fingerlings.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Efforts are also required to translate the lab trials to open waters.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: All in all, it is a huge science that the industry needs to finesse with the researchers, engineers and biologist experts.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: I seek the Minister to provide an update on the detailed plans of how aquaculture will support our "30 by 30" ambition.

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: To better support the industry, what is put in place to build the pipeline of researchers, technologists and industry partners to manage the trade?

speaker: Miss Cheryl Chan Wei Ling
text: Given our climate conditions which are different from those in temperate regions where aquaculture sector is more advanced, can the Minister explain how we are developing and applying learnings in this area for the tropics?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Can the Government elaborate on how our emerging aquaculture sector will contribute to Singapore's "30 by 30" goal?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: How is the Government ensuring that the environmental sustainability of our sea space is considered as Singapore embarks on the development of our aquaculture sector?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: In countries such as Japan, the three Ps collectively take pride in their local produce with consumers prepared to pay a premium to support good quality local produce.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: What can the Government do to help our local farms garner sufficient demand and support for local produce?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Are our Government agencies such as MINDEF army camps and Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA)'s Prisons able to take up the lead in supporting local produce in their F&B procurement?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Is the SFA considering any enhancements to the food hygiene and safety framework, including the points demerit system so as to encourage food business owners to maintain a hygienic and clean environment?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, being a small city-state, Singapore is not shielded from the impact of climate change.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The average temperature has increased, rainfall has become more unpredictable and intense in recent years.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore will remain more vulnerable to worsening climate changes.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government has taken the lead in advocating for a climate-resilient Singapore with adaptation efforts, one including protecting Singapore from sea level rise.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given that there can be drastic climate effects in a short period of time, what are the plans to ensure that infrastructure planning is capable to meet with these changes?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Second, MSE's publicly available information shared about the development of engineering projects for coastal protection measures.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What would be the scope in engineering solutions and the timeline that MSE is looking at?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In addition, will MSE work with relevant Ministries on creating new job opportunities and local business capabilities for these projects?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Lastly, our national agenda on building a climate-resilient nation requires a strategic financial plan to ensure that monetary resources are well spent on long-term benefits.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, how will these infrastructure-related project costs be financed?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We have built walls and stone embankments covering 70% to 80% of our coastline.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We have seen local institutions working together to research on coastal protection measures, using mangroves and other sea grasses as natural barriers to provide protection from the effects of climate change.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We have several beautiful beach parks from Changi to East Coast and West Coast, from Pasir Ris to Sembawang, not to mention many more offshore islands.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I will just pick one area, that is the East Coast Park, which has seen many efforts being put in place to stem the erosion of the sandbanks and wave breakers.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: So, we have very good reasons to be concerned about rising sea levels.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Minister update us on our progress to safeguard Singapore against the threat of rising sea levels and also the effort in coastal protection?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: This will also provide great opportunities to reimagine, reshape our coastlines and, at the same time, integrate amenities for human activities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Ministry involve the public in the design of Singapore's coastal protection measures so that they have a sense of ownership in managing climate change as well as the design of our future beach parks?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: In my Budget debate speech, I have also urged the Government to bring forward the timeline to build the podders and seawalls that were announced by the Prime Minister during the 2019 National Day Rally.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: As we face more complex challenges, there is a need to seek out innovative ideas, consult and co-create with stakeholders, including the public.

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Could MSE share how can the public, including youths, be involved in the design of Singapore's coastal protection measures, including nature-based solutions?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: Beyond public consultations for the design of coastal protection measures, how else does MSE engage with the people sector to empower individuals to take action towards our overall environmental goals, including, for example, on marine litter.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: These investments include both the creation of new knowledge through research as well as the implementation of solutions.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: How is the Government ensuring that there is adequate coordination of these multiple and concurrent efforts, especially in terms of the need to avoid duplication, ensure complementarity and appropriately phase the implementation of solutions that should be informed by the new science we have also invested in creating?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Poh Li San, both your cuts, please.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With about one third of our land less than five metres above sea level, coastal and flood protection is a necessary defence against the effects of global warming.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Do we have the time and the capacity to test out potential solutions?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry share an update on how we are building up research, innovation and engineering capabilities to apply against the threat of rising sea levels?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How are we collaborating in terms of research and exploration of new ideas with other countries in the same predicament?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: How can we involve members of the public, Government agencies, research centres and the private sector to tap upon their collective suggestions for solutions and measures to protect our coastal areas?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: With climate change, we are also experiencing more intense rainfall.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry share more about PUB's plans to develop flood protection measures and integrate these with coastal protection?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Over the years, dengue remains as one of the biggest public health threats.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: In 2022, there were 19 dengue deaths – four times more than 2021.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: I understand that quite a number of estates had asked when Project Wolbachia will be extended to more areas, especially for their areas.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry share how successful has this project been in areas where it had been launched?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: It takes time and resources to breed this special type of male mosquitoes.

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Would the Ministry share an update on the progress of Project Wolbachia?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: Will the programme be extended to more areas in the near future?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: If so, what are NEA's plans to scale up production of Wolbachia bacteria-carrying male mosquitoes?

speaker: Ms Poh Li San
text: What are the key challenges faced in strengthening our public health defences?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As such, some of us may have a complacent mindset and overlook the fact that the dengue virus is debilitating and can be fatal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Clearly, a multi-pronged approach is urgently needed to tackle the environmental factors of mosquito breeding, alongside medical solutions or precautions to better protect people living in Singapore from this scourge.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On eradicating mosquito breeding, we owe our gratitude to the teams deployed by NEA for their intense ground inspections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There may be some inspection fatigue felt by residents living in dengue clusters as they are subject to repeated inspections.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, these checks are needed for public health and the well-being of the community.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Apart from source eradication, what is the state of the other strategies?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, Project Wolbachia has been around since 2016 and expanded in phases.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given that it takes at least a year from the Wolbachia-Aedes mosquito release to suppress the mosquito population, how long will it take for Project Wolbachia to cover all residential areas?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As for vaccinations, I note from a Parliamentary answer in July 2022 to my colleague Ms He Ting Ru that there are about six vaccine candidates in development.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is the status of its evaluation by the Health Sciences Authority (HSA)?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For our residents, seeking treatment first at the nearest general practitioner (GP) clinic is the quickest option.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: How high is the threshold for symptoms before a dengue blood test is conducted?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also understand that these tests are not cheap and I would ask the Government to consider a subsidy for such tests if a doctor deems it fit to order them.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am glad that Nee Soon East was one of the pilot sites for Project Wolbachia.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I remember walking around the estate with a container of live male mosquitoes to show residents that male mosquitoes do not bite.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am quite sure many residents thought I was crazy and that I have finally really lost it.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It was extremely difficult to explain why we were releasing mosquitoes to reduce the mosquito population.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It just did not make sense for many residents but they trust that we were doing the right thing and supported this innovative project.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I am very glad that the results of Project Wolbachia have been so positive.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: This project has been vital in combating dengue and saving lives.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: On behalf of Nee Soon East residents, I thank MSE and NEA for launching this project.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: I have seen first-hand how effective Project Wolbachia is.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: It should be expanded to more areas in Singapore – in fact, all areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on the progress of Project Wolbachia and the timelines for this project to be extended throughout Singapore?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: How many sites is Project Wolbachia currently deployed at and would this programme be expanded to more sites as one of the measures to combat dengue?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Woodgrove's Division Zone 3, 5 and 6 were part of Project Wolbachia.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: The releases were expected to reduce the dengue vector in these high-risk areas and to help understand the impact of Wolbachia technology on dengue cases.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: What is the finding and progress of Project Wolbachia so far?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Will the programme be extended to more areas across Singapore?

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: During the peak of dengue seasons last year, none of my 11 zones in Woodgrove were spared, despite community efforts during our regular town halls to raise awareness on dengue prevention.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: I therefore hope that Project Wolbachia can be extended to the other eight zones in Woodgrove, especially to those places with more seniors and families with young children.

speaker: Ms Hany Soh
text: Apart from Project Wolbachia, what other measures can be further implemented to minimise the risk of Singaporeans contracting dengue fever?

text: These community and youth-focused grants include the 3P Partnership Fund, Call for Ideas Fund, SG Eco Fund, Young ChangeMakers Grant and even the Youth Action Challenge.

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Has the Government assessed the effectiveness of such grants across the whole-of-Government?

speaker: Prof Koh Lian Pin
text: Will the findings be shared with the public?

speaker: Ms Nadia Ahmad Samdin
text: We need more of such ground-up initiatives led by and in the community.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Chairman, before I address the cuts filed by Members, I would like to thank many Members who spoke on sustainability during the Budget debate.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In particular, Prof Koh Lian Pin's call for climate change and sustainability to always be among the bread-and-butter issues we focus on.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And Ms Carrie Tan's motto to Share More, Use Less, Waste Not, resonated with me.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean also spoke about our raised climate ambition and the urgent need for climate action.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: He explained that a whole-of-nation effort was needed to transition to a greener future.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This nationwide effort is underpinned by the Singapore Green Plan 2030, which we launched two years ago.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Green Plan charts bold and concrete policies and actions for Singapore to achieve our net-zero emissions goal.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It serves as a critical compass on our path to sustainability.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: My colleagues from other Ministries have been or will be providing updates on their green plan initiatives over the Committee of Supply (COS) debate.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must press on with this intergenerational effort to steward a green, liveable and climate-resilient home for Singaporeans and our future generations.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Today, my colleagues from the Ministry of Sustainability and the Environment (MSE) and I will share how we are laying the foundations for a green nation that is Climate-Resilient and Climate-Friendly.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: First, I will elaborate on how we are leading, enabling and facilitating Singapore's transition to a climate-friendly nation.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The public sector will lead the way for Singapore's decarbonisation journey and pave the way for green efforts to take root.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Prof Koh Lian Pin and Mr Don Wee asked for a progress update.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To spearhead the effort, we have appointed Singapore's first Government Chief Sustainability Officer (GCSO).

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Each Ministry has also appointed a Chief Sustainability Officer to oversee sustainability matters across their Ministry family.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They will work closely with the GCSO to develop and coordinate strategies to meet this ambition.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our public sector agencies are pushing ahead with decarbonising their systems and processes.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For instance, the National Environment Agency (NEA) is working with Keppel Seghers on a joint feasibility study to capture carbon dioxide emitted from Waste-to-Energy plants.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Poh Li San asked about PUB's decarbonisation plans and solutions.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: PUB has also committed to achieve net-zero emissions around 2045, in line with our GreenGov.SG ambition.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Their decarbonisation strategy is underpinned by 3Rs – Reduce, Replace and Remove.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: PUB's upcoming Tuas Water Reclamation Plant (WRP) will be fully energy self-sufficient by harnessing synergies with NEA's Integrated Waste Management Facility.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Next, PUB will also replace carbon-based energy sources with renewable energy, including solar.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are already home to one of the world's largest floating solar farms at Tengeh Reservoir.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are deploying the next floating solar farms at Pandan Reservoir and plan to call the tender for this later this year.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: PUB is also exploring innovative technologies to remove carbon.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In partnership with the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), PUB is test-bedding the use of novel electrolysis technology to capture carbon dioxide in seawater as part of the desalination process.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will produce hydrogen and pre-treated seawater so that it can be desalinated at lower energy.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will start with reporting Scope 1 and 2 emissions, electricity and water consumption with reference to international standards and frameworks.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: From FY2024, all Statutory Boards will also make their annual environmental sustainability disclosures.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Several statutory boards have started making sustainability disclosures.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They have been systematically incorporating sustainability in their decision-making and risk management frameworks to achieve concrete sustainability outcomes.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As Mr Don Wee, Mr Louis Ng and Prof Koh pointed out, the public sector can drive the nation's transition to a green economy by leveraging on its procurement budget.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The public sector has adopted green procurement since 2007.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Thus far, we have introduced sustainability requirements for selected goods and services.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, Information and Communications Technology (ICT) equipment, electrical appliances and printing paper must first meet environmental standards before they are assessed on price and quality attributes.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Building on this foundation, we intend to raise the bar.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Such projects include public infrastructure, industrial buildings and office ICT equipment contracts.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Using ICT as an example, in addition to the requirement of matching the best-in-class in energy efficiency, we may evaluate the efforts of the tenderers in reducing packaging and carbon footprint of their operations, when we evaluate the tender bids.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will review the amount and engage industry closely as we expand the adoption of sustainability criteria to more public sector procurement sectors.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Don Wee asked if such efforts to green the public sector will entail additional costs.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Environmental sustainability is not costless and we will have to pay a bit more for greener goods and services.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: But as the world decarbonises, the demand for green products and services will grow.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And green procurement in the public sector will encourage suppliers to adopt sustainability practices and develop green products and services.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Thereby, enhancing the growth of the green economy in Singapore and the competitiveness of our companies globally.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) had outlined initiatives that support businesses in adopting sustainability practices, such as measuring carbon emissions sustainability reporting and seizing opportunities in the green economy.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I hope that these initiatives under GreenGov.SG will spur many in the private sector to follow suit, in publishing their own sustainability reports and incorporating sustainability considerations in their procurement policies.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Together as a nation, we can transform our economy.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This leads me to talk about enabling the transformation through partnering businesses and the community.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Building a green nation requires the participation of all – businesses, communities and persons.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government cannot do it alone and all of us must work closely alongside each other, as partners, to deliver on the Green Plan.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will be raising our carbon tax progressively over the next few years to further incentivise carbon and energy efficiency throughout the economy and society.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) had addressed queries on allowances under the transition framework that Miss Cheryl Chan asked about.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Creating more products and services with less resources and less waste will raise their competitiveness in the long run, particularly against higher carbon and energy prices.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Businesses must invest in energy efficient equipment or manufacturing processes.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: However, over the long run, lower energy and resource use will lead to lower costs over the equipment's lifecycle.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh asked about the support provided for businesses, including SMEs, in making this upfront investment.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We recognise that upfront capital investment can be challenging for our businesses, particularly SMEs.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To support an inclusive transition, we will help SMEs make the switch.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Enterprise Singapore introduced the Energy Efficiency Grant (EEG) for food services, food manufacturing and retail sectors last year.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NEA also enhanced the Energy Efficiency Fund (E2F) for manufacturing companies to invest in energy efficient equipment.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: One SME that benefited from the enhanced E2F is ACP Metal Finishing Private Limited (ACP), which specialises in metal surface treatments and finishes.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: ACP tapped on the enhanced E2F to replace over a thousand fluorescent lightings in its facilities with more energy efficient LED lightings.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will also further simplify the grant application process by streamlining the measurement and verification requirements.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I encourage eligible companies, particularly our SMEs to tap the enhanced scheme to defray the cost of switching to more energy efficient equipment.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will enhance their competitiveness, as they participate in the greening of our economy.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Gan and Dr Lim Wee Kiak also called for support for households to be more energy efficient.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: With rising number of households, more working from home and usage of appliances, increasing energy efficiency in our homes is more important than ever.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our energy labels, with the number of ticks, have enabled consumers to make informed decisions when purchasing appliances.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I am heartened that more consumers are choosing appliances with higher energy efficiency.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Suppliers have noticed this and are responding by expanding their offering of energy efficient appliances.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will add energy labels to portable air-conditioners and more types of lamps next year.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The standards of air-conditioners, refrigerators, lamps and televisions will also be raised over the next two years to lock in efficiency gains and remove less efficient appliances from the market.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These will help to further reduce energy consumption in our households and help consumers reduce their utility bills by choosing more energy efficient appliances.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: (In Mandarin):   We recognise that purchasing energy efficient appliances may involve some additional costs upfront, in order to benefit from lower utility bills in the long run.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For example, last year, a family bought a 3-tick refrigerator that cost about $800.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A comparable 2-tick model would cost about $200 less.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have been working with community partners to increase awareness of the Programme, through outreach activities to residents, posters at community clubs, and digital display panels at HDB blocks.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have also worked with retailers to display CFH Programme collaterals on eligible appliances for easy identification and reminder.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will enable more households to be eligible for the scheme, to tap on the vouchers and to benefit from bigger savings in their utility bills.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: (In English): Aside from increasing efficiency, circularity is another avenue of being climate-friendly.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Minister of State Amy Khor will elaborate further on our efforts towards a zero waste nation, in particular, to reduce packaging waste and boost our recycling rate.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: She will also share about continued efforts to partner hawkers in ensuring Singapore's treasured hawker culture is safeguarded for years to come.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Grants and policies are but tools and enablers.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To unlock the next bound of the green transition, we must change our collective mindsets and behaviours.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Individually, our actions may feel insignificant, but collectively, we can build a new social compact necessary for a green Singapore.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government has been facilitating the green transition through our engagements and partnerships with the community under our Forward Singapore Steward Pillar.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: He will be heartened to hear that many Singaporeans share our ambitions and hopes for a greener Singapore and have great ideas to help us get there.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To date, over 1,400 Singaporeans ranging from the youth to the elderly have attended close to 20 engagement sessions under the Forward Singapore Steward Pillar.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The engagements focused on the challenges and trade-offs in fiscal and environmental sustainability topics, such as our net-zero ambition, resource circularity, coastal and flood resilience and food security.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In a dialogue with seniors at Toa Payoh, I was particularly inspired by their ideas and enthusiasm towards recycling and reducing their carbon footprint.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I remember Mr Wang, who sold his car and switched to cycling after the completion of a MRT station in his neighbourhood.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: He is also a handyman, repairing discarded electrical appliances regularly for his neighbours to reuse.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We can certainly take a leaf out of the book of these residents in embodying the spirit of stewardship.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In a bid to turn more of these ideas into action, we have launched the Green Nation Pledge.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are calling on individuals and organisations to pledge as a contributor, advocate or champion.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: My Ministry will continue to facilitate ground-up sustainability initiatives and partner the community in building a green nation.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Senior Parliamentary Secretary Baey will share more on our efforts in his speech and also about our efforts on public health resilience.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Chairman, the latest Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) report found that the Southeast Asia region is one of the most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Rising sea levels pose an existential threat to us.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are especially at risk as a low-lying island state.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We also expect significant increases in temperature and extreme weather patterns by the end of the century.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The impacts of climate change are far-reaching and have downstream implications on food security when harvests are affected and on water security when sources of water dry up during heatwaves.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: My Ministry is laying the foundation for Singapore to be a climate-ready nation.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I will elaborate on how we will bolster our water security and Senior Minister of State Koh Poh Koon will share how we are shoring up our coastal defences, inland flood protection and food resilience.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Singapore has four national taps – water from local catchments, imported water, NEWater and desalinated water.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In addressing the threats of climate change, we will invest further in these weather-resilient taps.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Ms Poh has asked for an update on our water infrastructure.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will increase the capacity and efficiency of desalination capabilities.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Last year, we opened our fifth desalination plant – the Jurong Island Desalination Plant (JIDP).

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is co-located with the Tembusu Multi-Utilities Complex (TMUC).

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This enables the plant to be about 5% more energy efficient compared to earlier desalination plants.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will strengthen our systems for managing used water and recycling it into NEWater.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Used water is a precious resource that can be recycled endlessly to fortify our water resilience.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We capture our used water through our Deep Tunnel Sewerage System (DTSS) – a network of deep tunnels that form a superhighway for our used water.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The used water travels through the DTSS by gravity to Water Reclamation Plants (WRPs) and NEWater factories.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They are then collected, treated and reclaimed to produce NEWater.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will connect the existing Changi WRP on the eastern side and the upcoming Tuas WRP in the west.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will be redeveloping the Kranji Water Reclamation Plant and NEWater Factory in the north as the new piece of our three-node DTSS.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Together, these developments will strengthen Singapore's water reclamation system, increase the treatment capacity of used water and bolster our NEWater production.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Efforts to secure our water supply must be accompanied by efforts to manage our water demand.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Mr Gan asked about our efforts in improving water efficiency in the non-domestic sector.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The non-domestic sector currently accounts for more than half of our total water demand and can play a big part in water conservation.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We have required large water users to establish water management systems and submit annual plans for water efficiency to PUB, under the Mandatory Water Efficiency Management Practices.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Through this exercise, large water users are made aware of water intensive parts of their operations and identify opportunities to increase efficiency.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These are namely the wafer fabrication, electronics and biomedical industries.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They are water intensive and have high potential for water recycling.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Households can play a part through sustainable living practices and being mindful of our consumption.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is easy to take for granted that clean water is available in every household today.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It is unfathomable that 60 years ago, water rationing was imposed in Singapore.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The water supply had to be cut off for 12 hours, three times a week, for about eight months.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must, therefore, continue to promote water conservation among our population.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A resilient water supply is critical in safeguarding our water needs from external shocks arising from climate and environmental impacts.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Singapore Water Story is one that must carry through to future generations.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: And that is the goal of a green nation: to steward a green, liveable and climate-resilient home.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A home that is sustainable and will last for generations.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Government will lay the foundations for a green Singapore that is climate-friendly and climate-ready, but we will only make headway if this is a shared vision and if we all take collective steps along this journey.

speaker: ﻿The Minister for Sustainability and the Environment (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
